Geometry | Quarter 2 | Unit 4: Quadrilaterals and Polygons

The Four-Bar Linkage

How does a suspension link keep its shape while it moves?

Duration
50 minutes
Grade level
Grades 9–10
Topic
Parallelograms
Standards
HSG-CO.C.11, HSG-GPE.B.4, HSG-GPE.B.5

Students use the side, angle and diagonal properties of parallelograms, prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, check parallelograms on a coordinate grid, and model a moving four-bar linkage.

2Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  • Use the properties of parallelograms to find sides, angles and diagonals.
  • Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
  • Check whether a quadrilateral is a parallelogram on a coordinate grid.
  • Explain why a parallelogram linkage keeps opposite sides parallel as it moves.

3Essential question

What has to be true for four bars to always form a parallelogram?

5MTB connection

Many rear suspension designs are four-bar linkages: the front triangle, two links and the rear triangle pivot together. When opposite bars are equal, the linkage is a parallelogram and the rear piece moves up and down without tilting.

Real designs usually change the bar lengths slightly on purpose, so the shape changes as the suspension compresses; that tunes how the bike pedals and brakes.

The mathOn the trail
ParallelogramA linkage with equal opposite bars
Opposite sides stay parallelThe connecting bar doesn’t rotate
Consecutive angles supplementaryOne pivot angle opens as its neighbour closes
Diagonals bisectA check builders can measure

7MTB activity

MTB Classroom Activity

Suspension Linkage Lab

Build and measure a parallelogram four-bar linkage to see which properties stay true as it moves.

You’ll need: Card strips: two 12 cm and two 8 cm per pair, plus one extra 10 cm strip; Paper fasteners; Protractor and ruler
